summary.text: Earth's crust is the planet's outer shell of rock, making up less than one percent of its radius and volume.
Both continental and oceanic crust are less dense than the mantle, so both float on it, and the thicker, lighter continental crust rides higher.
Ocean crust is constantly made at spreading centers and destroyed at subduction zones, so the oldest is only about 200 million years old, while most continental crust is much older.

facts.label: Most abundant mineral
facts.value: Feldspars, about 41% of continental crust by mass

items.prompt: Continents stand as high ground while the ocean floor lies in deep basins. What causes this difference in height?

options.label: Ocean water weighs the seafloor down
Continents are made of denser rock
Waves have worn the seafloor away
Continental crust is thicker and more buoyant

items.explain: The thicker, less dense continental crust is more buoyant on the mantle, so its surface sits higher than ocean crust.

items.prompt: Why doesn't Earth's crust sink down into the mantle beneath it?

options.label: The crust is welded to the core
The mantle is denser than the crust
The crust is held up by trapped gas
The mantle is too cold to move

items.explain: The upper mantle is denser than the crust, so the crust stays on top and floats.

items.prompt: A geologist wants to watch brand-new crust being formed. Where should she go?

options.label: A mid-ocean spreading center
A deep ocean trench
The middle of an old continent
A shallow coastal shelf

items.explain: At mid-ocean spreading centers, partly melted mantle yields basalt magma that forms new ocean crust; trenches are where crust sinks.

items.prompt: The seafloor is constantly being made, yet none of it is very old. What keeps ocean crust young?

options.label: Ocean water slowly dissolves it
Coral reefs grow over it
Old ocean crust sinks back into the mantle
Sediment piles turn it into continent

items.explain: New crust forming at spreading centers is balanced by old crust sinking at subduction zones, so the oldest is about 200 million years old.

items.prompt: Earth's very first crust formed as the young planet cooled. Why can't geologists find any of it today?

options.label: It lies buried under polar ice
Erosion, impacts and plate motion destroyed it
It sank all the way into the core
It never fully hardened into rock

items.explain: None of the primary crust survives; all of it was destroyed by erosion, impacts and plate tectonics.

items.prompt: In the upper part of the crust, a mine shaft is dug one kilometer deeper. Locally, how much hotter can the rock get?

options.label: No warmer at all
Under 1 °C warmer
About 300 °C warmer
Up to about 30 °C warmer

items.explain: Temperature rises with depth, by as much as 30 °C for every kilometer locally in the upper crust.

pack.title: Why the Seafloor Stays Young
pack.question: Why is ocean crust young while continental crust can be billions of years old?

beats.title: Why the Seafloor Stays Young
beats.hook: Some continental rocks are at least 3.7 billion years old, yet the oldest ocean floor is only about 200 million years old.

beats.prompt: New ocean crust keeps forming at mid-ocean spreading centers, day after day. What has to happen somewhere else?
beats.explain: Because new crust is always being made, old crust must be destroyed: at subduction zones, ocean plates sink back into the mantle.

choices.label: Old ocean crust sinks back into the mantle
The oldest crust melts away under seawater
choices.feedback: Seawater does not remove the crust; it is destroyed by sinking.

choices.label: The planet slowly swells to make room
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the new crust is balanced elsewhere rather than making Earth bigger.

choices.label: The new crust piles up into mountains at the ridge
choices.feedback: The ridge keeps spreading apart; the old crust is not stacked up there.

beats.prompt: Sort each feature into the type of crust it describes.

left.label: Mostly felsic rock such as granite
Rocks as old as about 4.28 billion years
Oldest is only about 200 million years

beats.explain: Continental crust is thick, light and ancient; oceanic crust is thin, denser and constantly renewed.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in Earth's early history in order.

items.label: Rocky bodies collide and stick, building the planet
The heat melts early Earth completely
Earth cools and forms a primary crust
Secondary and tertiary crust form, as ocean and continental crust

beats.explain: Accretion made so much heat that Earth melted; as it cooled a first crust formed, and since then ocean and continental crust have been forming.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?

steps.text: Both kinds of crust are less dense than the mantle.
So both kinds of crust float on the mantle.
Continental crust is thicker and less dense than oceanic crust.
So the ocean crust's surface sits higher than the continents.

beats.explain: The thicker, less dense continental crust is more buoyant, so continents sit higher and the ocean basins lie low.

beats.idea: Ocean crust is endlessly made at spreading centers and swallowed at subduction zones, while lighter continental crust floats high and lasts.
